steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our database theory paper on the complexity of Shapley value computation for queries, showing it reduces from probabilistic query evaluation and model counting. Include background, the open question, and a Contributions subsection.

## Contributions
- Specialized problems SPQE, SPPQE, FMC, FGMC

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Shapley value is a well-known measure for distributing wealth among players in cooperative games. It has many desirable properties and has been applied in many areas, including databases, where it gives a natural way to quantify the contribution of a database element (typically a tuple) to a query result. The problem of Shapley value computation (SVC) for database queries has got a lot of attention lately. It is known to be computationally challenging – \#\textsf{P} -hard and \textsf{FP}^{\#\textsf{P}} -complete in data complexity under polynomial-time reductions – and so the question is which queries have tractable SVC (i.e., in FP). Previous work has conjectured that a FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomy holds for unions of conjunctive queries, like the one for query evaluation in tuple-independent probabilistic databases and for the generalized model counting problem. Right now the conjecture has only been confirmed for the subclass of self-join-free conjunctive queries (sjf-CQs). But there has been progress on the complexity of SVC for other query classes, and FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomies have been proven for sjf-CQs with safe negations and for regular path queries.

The SVC dichotomy for sjf-CQs established in earlier work identifies exactly the same tractable queries (the hierarchical ones) as the dichotomies for probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) and generalized model counting (GMC), even though it was obtained by different means. This raised the interesting question of whether the Shapley dichotomy follows from these existing dichotomies, and more generally what the precise relationship between these problems is. Subsequent work gave a partial answer with a general polynomial-time reduction (for all queries, not just sjf-CQs) from SVC to PQE, which shows how tractability results for PQE can be transferred to SVC.

Can hardness results for SVC be explained in the same way via PQE or GMC? A recent result showed even more how close the settings are, by reproving the hardness of SVC with the same model counting problem for Boolean functions that was originally used to show hardness of PQE for non-hierarchical sjf-CQs. But a reduction from PQE or GMC to SVC has not been exhibited yet, probably because SVC outputs a complex weighted sum that cannot obviously be used for probability or model counting computations. Our paper looks at this missing link and shows that the matching dichotomy conditions are not a coincidence, because there are reductions from PQE and GMC to SVC for broad classes of queries, which explain the existing hardness results for SVC and also give some new complexity results.

## Contributions

- Section 3: SPQE and SPPQE (restricted fact probabilities); polynomial-time equivalent to FMC and FGMC; Figure 1(a)
  - previously implicit / related settings; brings clarity; analogues of SVC
  - existing SVC -> PQE reduction really goes to FGMC and SPPQE
- Sections 4-5: first reductions FGMC (equivalently SPPQE) -> SVC
  - Lemmas 4.1, 4.7, 4.9; (C -)homomorphism-closed queries
  - often query-preserving: {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{FGMC}_{q}}{}{} to {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{SVC}_{q}}{}{}; equivalence for a range of query classes
- Consequences
  - FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomies for sjf-CQ s and regular path queries as corollaries
  - new dichotomies: constant-free unions of connected CQs, connected homomorphism-closed graph queries (Figure 1(b))
- Section 6: no exogenous facts; safe negation; maximum Shapley value; Shapley value of constants

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The Shapley value is a well-known measure for distributing wealth among players in cooperative games. It has many desirable properties and has been applied in many areas, including databases, where it gives a natural way to quantify the contribution of a database element (typically a tuple) to a query result. Previous work has conjectured that a FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomy holds for unions of conjunctive queries, like the one for query evaluation in tuple-independent probabilistic databases and for the generalized model counting problem. Right now the conjecture has only been confirmed for the subclass of self-join-free conjunctive queries (sjf-CQs). But there has been progress on the complexity of SVC for other query classes, and FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomies have been proven for sjf-CQs with safe negations and for regular path queries.

The SVC dichotomy for sjf-CQs established in earlier work identifies exactly the same tractable queries (the hierarchical ones) as the dichotomies for probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) and generalized model counting (GMC), even though it was obtained by different means. This raised the interesting question of whether the Shapley dichotomy follows from these existing dichotomies, and more generally what the precise relationship between these problems is. Subsequent work gave a partial answer with a general polynomial-time reduction (for all queries, not just sjf-CQs) from SVC to PQE, which shows how tractability results for PQE can be transferred to SVC.

Can hardness results for SVC be explained in the same way via PQE or GMC? A recent result showed even more how close the settings are, by reproving the hardness of SVC with the same model counting problem for Boolean functions that was originally used to show hardness of PQE for non-hierarchical sjf-CQs. But a reduction from PQE or GMC to SVC has not been exhibited yet, probably because SVC outputs a complex weighted sum that cannot obviously be used for probability or model counting computations. Our paper looks at this missing link and shows that the matching dichotomy conditions are not a coincidence, because there are reductions from PQE and GMC to SVC for broad classes of queries, which explain the existing hardness results for SVC and also give some new complexity results.

## Contributions

Our first conceptual contribution (Section 3) is to introduce specializations of the PQE problem, SPQE and SPPQE, which we get by restricting the probability values of facts, and to show that they are polynomial-time equivalent to variants FMC and FGMC of the model counting MC and generalized model counting GMC problems (cf. “model counting” and “probabilistic evaluation” boxes of Figure 1(a)). Some of these problems were used implicitly in proofs before, or defined for related settings, but formally introducing them in the database setting brings some clarity and order to the literature and gives us analogues of SVC in the probabilistic and counting domains. In fact the existing reduction of SVC to PQE can be expressed more precisely as a reduction to the more restricted FGMC and SPPQE problems.

Our main technical contributions (presented in Section 4 and proven in Section 5) are the first known reductions in the other direction: from FGMC (equivalently, SPPQE) to SVC. We give three such reductions (Lemmas 4.1, 4.7 and 4.9), and each uses somewhat different structural conditions and covers different classes of (C -)homomorphism-closed queries. Importantly, in many cases our reductions preserve the query, i.e. reduce {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{FGMC}_{q}}{}{} to {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{SVC}_{q}}{}{}. So we establish the polynomial-time equivalence of {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{FGMC}_{q}}{}{} and {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{SVC}_{q}}{}{} for a range of query classes, which is strong new evidence that SVC is nothing more than a counting problem.

Because of our reductions, the FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomies for SVC for sjf-CQ s and regular path queries can now be obtained as corollaries of existing dichotomies for PQE and GMC (intuitively, by following the arrows in Figure 1(a) from and to known results). Also, since our lemma hypotheses are general, new results can be obtained too. In particular we establish FP / \#\textsf{P} dichotomies for constant-free unions of connected CQs and connected homomorphism-closed graph queries. These results are in Section 4 and summarized in Figure 1(b).

In Section 6 we show that our proof techniques are useful in other scenarios too. First, essentially the same reductions, with an additional hypothesis, can show hardness of Shapley value computation over databases without assumed (“ exogenous ”) facts (existing reductions crucially use the presence of “exogenous” facts). Second, a simple adaptation of our techniques partially recaptures existing results for CQs with safe negation. Third, computing the maximum Shapley value is just as hard as SVC as far as our reductions go. Finally, we start the study of the Shapley value of database constants (instead of facts) and use our methods to show how this problem can be formally related to the analogous model counting problems.

steps.text:
The Shapley value [1] is a well-known measure for distributing wealth among players in cooperative games. It enjoys many desirable properties and has found application in numerous areas, including databases, where it provides a natural means of quantifying the contribution of a database element (typically a tuple) to a query result. The problem of Shapley value computation (SVC) for database queries has received considerable attention lately [2,3,4,5,6]. It is known to be computationally challenging – \#\textsf{P} -hard and \textsf{FP}^{\#\textsf{P}} -complete in data complexity under polynomial-time reductions – which motivates the question of identifying the queries for which SVC is tractable (i.e., in FP). It has been conjectured [4,5] that a FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomy holds for unions of conjunctive queries, as is the case for query evaluation in tuple-independent probabilistic databases [7] and for the generalized model counting problem [8]. At present, this conjecture has only been confirmed for the subclass of self-join-free conjunctive queries (sjf-CQs) [2]. There has, however, been progress on classifying the complexity of SVC for other query classes, with FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomies proven for sjf-CQs with safe negations [6] and for regular path queries [3].

The dichotomy established in [2] for SVC for sjf-CQs identifies precisely the same tractable queries (the hierarchical ones) as the dichotomies for probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) and generalized model counting (GMC), despite having been obtained through different means. This raised the intriguing question of whether the Shapley dichotomy is a consequence of these existing dichotomies and, more generally, what precise relationship holds between these problems. Subsequent work [4] provided a partial answer by exhibiting a general polynomial-time reduction (for all queries, not just sjf-CQs) of SVC to PQE, showing how tractability results for PQE can be transferred to SVC.

Can hardness results for SVC similarly be explained via PQE or GMC? A recent result [5] further demonstrated the closeness of the settings by reproving the hardness of SVC using the same model counting problem for Boolean functions originally used to show hardness of PQE for non-hierarchical sjf-CQs [11]. However, a reduction from PQE or GMC to SVC has yet to be exhibited, no doubt because SVC outputs a complex weighted sum that cannot obviously be employed for probability or model counting computations. Our paper investigates this missing link and shows that the matching dichotomy conditions are no coincidence: it is possible to exhibit reductions from PQE and GMC to SVC for broad classes of queries, which not only explain existing hardness results for SVC but also yield some new complexity results.

## Contributions

Our first conceptual contribution (Section 3) is to introduce suitable specializations of the PQE problem, namely SPQE and SPPQE, obtained by restricting the probability values of facts, and to show that they are polynomial-time equivalent to variants FMC and FGMC of the model counting MC and generalized model counting GMC problems (cf. “model counting” and “probabilistic evaluation” boxes of Figure 1(a)). While some of these problems had been used implicitly in proofs, or defined for related settings, their formal introduction in the database setting brings clarity and order to the literature and provides us with suitable analogues of SVC in the probabilistic and counting domains. Indeed, the existing reduction of SVC to PQE can more precisely be expressed as a reduction to the more restricted FGMC and SPPQE problems.

Our main technical contributions (presented in Section 4 and proven in Section 5) are the first known reductions in the opposite direction: from FGMC (equivalently, SPPQE) to SVC. We provide three such reductions (Lemmas 4.1, 4.7 and 4.9), each employing somewhat different structural conditions and covering different classes of (C -)homomorphism-closed queries. Importantly, in many cases our reductions preserve the query, i.e. reduce {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{FGMC}_{q}}{}{} to {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{SVC}_{q}}{}{}. We thereby establish the polynomial-time equivalence of {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{FGMC}_{q}}{}{} and {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\textup{SVC}_{q}}{}{} for a range of query classes, providing strong new evidence that SVC is nothing more than a counting problem.

As a consequence of our reductions, the FP / \#\textsf{P} -hard dichotomies for SVC for sjf-CQ s and regular path queries can now be obtained as corollaries of existing dichotomies for PQE and GMC (intuitively, by following the arrows in Figure 1(a) from and to known results). Moreover, owing to the general nature of our lemma hypotheses, additional new results can be obtained. In particular, we establish FP / \#\textsf{P} dichotomies for constant-free unions of connected CQs and connected homomorphism-closed graph queries. These results are presented in Section 4 and summarized in Figure 1(b).

In Section 6, we further demonstrate the utility of our proof techniques by applying them to other scenarios. First, we show that essentially the same reductions, modulo an additional hypothesis, can be used to show hardness of Shapley value computation over databases without assumed (“ exogenous ”) facts (existing reductions make crucial use of the presence of “exogenous” facts). Second, a simple adaptation of our techniques allows us to partially recapture existing results for CQs with safe negation [6]. Third, we show that computing the maximum Shapley value is just as hard as SVC as far as our reductions go. Finally, we initiate the study of the Shapley value of database constants (rather than facts) and use our methods to show how this problem can be formally related to the analogous model counting problems.
